papers.title: Sustained Activation of a Defensive Behavior-Related Circuit Elicits a distinct Homeostatic Sleep Response.
papers.abstract: Animals and humans often forgo sleep in response to other physiological needs. Prolonged wakefulness leads to a compensatory homeostatic sleep response involving enhanced amounts of sleep and electroencephalographic delta (0.5-4 Hz) power, yet how the type of preceding wakefulness and brain activity affects this response is poorly understood. Here we compared the pattern of brain activity and the homeostatic sleep response following sustained wakefulness induced by either gentle handling (GH), a widely used form of sleep deprivation in rodents; or optogenetic stimulation of neurons involved in avoidance/defensive responses, basal forebrain (BF) vesicular glutamatergic transporter type 2 (vGluT2) neurons. Local infusion of ionotropic glutamate receptor antagonists partially attenuated the wake-inducing effect of vGluT2-stimulation, but not that of GH, suggesting mediation by other non-glutamatergic BF subtypes. These antagonists also tended to produce more NREM sleep and a shorter NREM latency in the recovery period following vGluT2-stimulation. Both manipulations increased high theta (7-9 Hz) during wakefulness, an effect partially blocked by local infusion of the glutamate antagonist cocktail. Enhanced NREM sleep time and NREM delta power in the recovery period were more pronounced following GH than following vGluT2 stimulation. Whole-brain cFos immunohistochemistry revealed stronger neuronal activity in brain regions involved in stress and avoidance/defensive behaviors with vGluT2 stimulation, compared to GH. Our results demonstrate that activation of a brain system involved in defensive behavior (BF vGluT2) elicits a distinct and diminished homeostatic sleep response compared to GH, potentially an evolutionary sleep adaptation which would maintain vigilance in the face of an ongoing threat.

papers.title: Sleep disturbance and enhanced aggression after chronic mild stress in mice: Association with hypothalamic nerve growth factor.
papers.abstract: Chronic stress disrupts sleep and induces behavioural abnormalities. However, the mechanisms linking stress-related sleep disturbances to abnormal social behaviour are unclear. In this study, a predictable chronic mild stress (CMS) paradigm was used, in which male mice were housed on a wire mesh for 3 weeks. CMS mice (n = 7 per group) had reduced non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep and NREM slow-wave activity, and they had enhanced aggressive behaviour, whereas anxiety- and depression-related behavioural measures were not markedly altered. At the molecular level, CMS was associated with lower hypothalamic Ngf mRNA levels, and hypothalamic NGF protein levels were related to aggressive behaviour. Intracerebroventricular administration of NGF promoted sleep in control and CMS mice (n = 6-7 per group), but aggressive behaviour was suppressed only in CMS mice (n = 8 per group). These findings suggest that hypothalamic NGF may contribute to mechanisms that link chronic stress-related sleep disturbances with aggressive behaviour, although the precise downstream mechanisms are not known.

papers.title: Disrupted sleep-wake regulation in the MCI-Park mouse model of Parkinson's Disease
papers.abstract: Disrupted sleep has a profound adverse impact on lives of Parkinson's Disease (PD) patients and their caregivers. Sleep disturbances are exceedingly common in PD, with substantial heterogeneity in type, timing, and severity. Among the most common sleep-related symptoms reported by PD patients are insomnia, excessive daytime sleepiness, and sleep fragmentation, characterized by interruptions and decreased continuity of sleep. Alterations in brain wave activity, as measured on the electroencephalogram (EEG), also occur in PD, with changes in the pattern and relative contributions of different frequency bands of the EEG spectrum to overall EEG activity in different vigilance states consistently observed. The mechanisms underlying these PD-associated sleep-wake abnormalities are poorly understood, and they are ineffectively treated by conventional PD therapies. To help fill this gap in knowledge, a new progressive model of PD - the MCI-Park mouse- was studied. Near the transition to the parkinsonian state, these mice exhibited significantly altered sleep-wake regulation, including increased wakefulness, decreased non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, increased sleep fragmentation, reduced rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, and altered EEG activity patterns. These sleep-wake abnormalities mirror those identified in PD patients. Thus, this model may help elucidate the circuit mechanisms underlying sleep disruption in PD and identify targets for novel therapeutic approaches.

papers.title: Automated Sleep Staging Performance Across Two Experimental Sleep Manipulation Protocols in Adolescents.
papers.abstract: Automated sleep staging algorithms improve the scalability of polysomnography analysis in adolescent research but are primarily validated in undisturbed, single-night sleep recordings. It remains unclear whether these algorithms maintain performance when sleep architecture is experimentally manipulated. This study evaluated the validity of two popular automated sleep staging approaches across two distinct sleep manipulation paradigms in adolescents: a sleep restriction protocol (N=43, mean age [SD]=13.37[1.06] years; four nights including two sleep extension [10hr] and two restriction [4hr] nights) and a slow-wave sleep deprivation (SWSD) protocol (N=18, mean age [SD]=17.17[1.79] years; baseline, SWSD, and recovery nights). Automated sleep staging was performed using the POPulation-level Sleep Stager (POPS), the Yet Another Spindle Algorithm (YASA), and combined POPS+YASA. Manual polysomnography scoring by experienced sleep technicians served as the reference standard. Agreement was assessed using Cohen's κ, and stage-specific performance was evaluated using F1 scores and confusion matrices. Mixed-effects models tested differences in overall and stage-specific agreement across nights. All staging approaches demonstrated moderate-to-substantial agreement with manual scoring across manipulated sleep conditions (κ range=0.53-0.76). In the sleep restriction study, agreement was lower in restricted versus extended sleep (P<0.05), and agreement declined across restriction nights, with poorer Wake, N1, and N2 classification, while N3 remained preserved. In the SWSD study, overall agreement was lower on the SWSD night, with poorer N3 classification while other stages were preserved. Automated sleep staging performance may be less consistent in adolescents when sleep is curtailed or fragmented; future studies should develop and validate these algorithms under multiple sleep conditions.

papers.title: Sleep-like slow waves in wakefulness index post-stroke behavioural alterations.
papers.abstract: Increases in high-amplitude, low-frequency EEG oscillations during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep serve as markers of neuronal silencing, which disrupts functional connectivity and is associated with a loss of awareness and responsiveness. Cortical slowing likewise occurs during wakefulness, upon sleep deprivation, and accompanies performance deterioration. Recent work has revealed similar oscillations (termed 'sleep-like slow waves') following stroke in brain regions close or connected to a brain lesion, offering a plausible but untested mechanism for stroke-related behavioural impairment. Here, we simultaneously recorded EEG and behavioural performance while 30 unilateral stroke patients (12 left hemisphere, 18 right hemisphere) and 27 age-matched healthy adults completed a computerised perceptual decision-making task. Stroke patients had predominantly middle cerebral artery strokes (n=25), with a small subset of posterior cerebral artery (n=4), and anterior cerebral artery/middle cerebral artery (n=1) lesions. Sleep-like slow waves occurred more frequently in stroke patients relative to healthy controls, with limited spatial specificity when comparing patients with left and right lesion sites (more slow waves ipsilateral of the lesion). Furthermore, there was a significant correlation between slow wave occurrence and the accuracy and speed of perceptual reports in stroke patients, suggesting that variations in the occurrence of slow waves may contribute to cognitive heterogeneity post-stroke. As sleep-like slow waves predict deficits in perceptual decision-making following stroke, they represent a plausible mechanism of post-lesion functional network dysfunction extending beyond the damaged regions, thereby contributing to broader cognitive impairments.

papers.title: Detection of Spreading Depolarization with Noninvasive Electroencephalography.
papers.abstract: Spreading depolarizations (SDs) are waves of near-complete breakdown of the transmembrane ion gradients that underlie migraine aura and occur in patients with moderate-to-severe traumatic, ischemic or hemorrhagic brain injury. SDs are involved in primary and secondary brain injury. They are associated with poor neurological outcome and represent a modifiable therapeutic target. However, despite decades of investigation, SD detection still requires invasive subdural electrocorticography (ECoG) using an implanted subdural electrode strip, restricting monitoring to a small subset of neurosurgical patients. We developed WAVEFRONT, a noninvasive scalp electroencephalography (EEG) biomarker of SD based on spatiotemporal propagation characteristics of delta-band EEG activity. The biomarker was trained and validated using concurrent, multi-day scalp EEG and invasive subdural electrocorticography recordings from patients with traumatic brain injury (TBI), subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), or malignant hemispheric stroke (MHS) across three institutions. We assessed out-of-sample performance across institutions, diagnosis, and surgical approaches, as well as calibration, temporal synchrony, and spatial specificity relative to gold-standard SDs annotated on ECoG. Clinical utility was further evaluated in 607 patients comatose after cardiac arrest from the multicenter International Cardiac Arrest REsearch (I-CARE) consortium, a population in whom invasive monitoring is not performed. Outcome analyses excluded patients who died (Cerebral Performance Category [CPC] 5) because death may reflect decisions to withdraw life-sustaining treatment in addition to neurological injury. A total of 1,119 gold-standard SDs were annotated in 32 patients (TBI, n=17; SAH, n=12; MHS, n=3; range 0-187 SDs per patient). Across exhaustive cross-validation and institution-, diagnosis-, and surgical approach-based hold-out analyses, WAVEFRONT models trained on one set of patients consistently maintained high performance when evaluated in previously unseen out-of-group cohorts. At the optimal operating point, WAVEFRONT achieved a mean cross-validated true positive rate of 97.3±1% with a false positive rate of 6.0±0.5%, calculated over 2-min sliding windows with 30-s overlaps. The cumulative duration of WAVEFRONT detections within 30-hour windows strongly correlated with the number of SDs measured by invasive ECoG (R 2 =0.7411). Scalp-detected depressions were spatially consistent with the location of the invasive recording strip, and visual inspection demonstrated close temporal correspondence with invasive detections, including during SD clusters. External validation in the independent I-CARE cohort using WAVEFRONT trained on the invasive-monitoring cohort demonstrated significantly greater SD burden on day 3 of post-arrest EEG monitoring among patients with poor neurological outcome (CPC 3-4, n=29) than those with good outcome (CPC 1-2, n=225; p=0.007). Eight decades after Leão's description of SD in 1944, we propose and validate a noninvasive scalp EEG biomarker of SD. Consistent performance across institution-, diagnosis-, and surgical approach-based hold-out analyses, together with burden calibration, spatial specificity, and temporal synchrony with ECoG detections, supports the validity of the WAVEFRONT framework. The association of biomarker burden with neurologic outcome after cardiac arrest suggests that noninvasive monitoring may enable investigation of spreading depolarizations in populations where invasive monitoring is not feasible. Future studies should evaluate prospective performance, treatment responsiveness, and disease-specific associations of the SD biomarker with clinical outcome.

papers.title: Glial Control of Insomnia: Astrocyte-Microglia Interactions in Stress, Hyperarousal and Sleep Dysregulation.
papers.abstract: Insomnia is a highly prevalent and burdensome sleep disorder whose pathophysiology remains incompletely understood. While traditional models have emphasized neuronal hyperarousal, accumulating evidence indicates that glial cells-particularly astrocytes and microglia-play central and complementary roles in the regulation of sleep-wake dynamics and the persistence of chronic insomnia. This review synthesizes clinical, experimental and translational evidence supporting a dual regulatory framework in which astrocytes and microglia act as key integrators of stress signalling, neuroinflammation, synaptic plasticity and sleep homeostasis. Astrocytes emerge as primary modulators of metabolic and neuro-modulatory coupling within sleep-wake circuits, linking hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis activation to dysregulated adenosine signalling, excitatory-inhibitory imbalance, impaired glymphatic clearance and circadian misalignment. In parallel, microglia function as immune and synaptic sculptors, with chronic sleep disturbance biasing them toward maladaptive activation states characterized by altered cytokine release, disrupted synaptic pruning and stress hormone-dependent signalling cascades. Although direct glia-resolved evidence in human insomnia remains limited, convergent findings from neuroimaging, animal models and sleep-immune research support a coordinated stress-glia-insomnia axis. We further highlight mechanisms of astrocyte-microglia crosstalk, including purinergic signalling, inflammatory feedback loops and calcium-dependent network synchronization, which may stabilize pathological hyperarousal states. Finally, we discuss emerging glia-targeted therapeutic strategies and key translational challenges, emphasizing the need for cell-type-specific biomarkers, spatiotemporally precise interventions and personalized treatment frameworks.

papers.title: EEG-based deep learning estimates preterm infants' cerebral age: Contribution of slow-wave and cross-frequency coupling.
papers.abstract: Reliably estimating cerebral maturation in preterm newborns is crucial for early identification of atypical neurodevelopment. We developed a deep-learning framework using a convolutional neural network (CNN) to predict postmenstrual age (PMA) from spontaneous neural activity in EEG recordings of 165 healthy preterm infants (28-38 weeks PMA). The model achieved a mean absolute error of 0.75 ± 0.60 weeks, with 73.9% of prediction errors within one week. To identify key neurophysiological drivers, we systematically manipulated signal components. Results showed that removing low-frequency activity (<4 Hz) significantly degraded performance and disrupting phase-amplitude coupling selectively impaired prediction accuracy before 34 weeks PMA, while high-frequency activity (>12 Hz) had minimal impact. Our results demonstrate that maturation signatures are primarily driven by slow-wave dynamics and their hierarchical coupling with faster oscillations, which are fundamental hallmarks of early neurodevelopment.

papers.title: Sex differences in post-traumatic epileptogenesis and neurological dysfunction following traumatic brain injury.
papers.abstract: Post-traumatic epilepsy (PTE) is a disabling long-term consequence of traumatic brain injury (TBI), but the role of biological sex on epileptogenesis and recovery remains unclear. Here, we comprehensively characterized chronic PTE development and neurological outcomes in adult male and female mice after severe TBI by controlled cortical impact. Animals underwent continuous video-EEG monitoring for 120 days, serial behavioral, motor, and cognitive testing, and terminal histological assessment of neurodegeneration, neuroinflammation, neurogenesis, and circuit remodeling. Females had a lower incidence of PTE, lower cohort-level seizure burden, a higher seizure threshold, and fewer epileptiform discharges than males. The burden of epileptogenic biomarkers of ripples, fast-ripples, interictal-spikes, and sleep-spindles were also reduced or delayed in females than males. However, among female animals that developed PTE, seizure latency and ictal burden were comparable between sexes, indicating that female sex primarily reduced susceptibility to epilepsy rather than the severity of chronic epilepsy. Females experienced less post-injury health deterioration, recovered neurological and motor function more rapidly, and performed better in recognition-memory and spatial-learning tasks, although chronic cognitive deficits persisted. At 120 days, females showed greater hippocampus neuronal preservation and markedly attenuated astrogliosis and microgliosis than males. Nevertheless, both sexes nevertheless exhibited hippocampal principal neuron and parvalbumin(+) interneuron loss, reduced dentate gyrus neurogenesis, and mossy fiber remodeling. Collectively, these findings identify biological sex as a major determinant of post-traumatic disease trajectory, separating susceptibility to PTE from the severity of epilepsy once established. Sex-stratified outcomes may therefore improve biomarker development and guide sex-specific preventive therapies for PTE. This study reveals a female-resilient phenotype that limits epileptogenesis while leaving chronic network, cognitive deficits, and structural abnormalities unresolved after injury.

papers.title: Physiological Sleep Features Associated With Dimensions of Daily Dysfunction in Insomnia.
papers.abstract: Daily dysfunction is a key criterion of insomnia, but its underlying structure and relationship with objective sleep physiology remain unclear. This study aimed to identify the dimensions of subjective daily dysfunction using exploratory factor analysis (EFA) in individuals with insomnia and to examine its association with polysomnography (PSG) macroarchitecture, electroencephalographic (EEG) spectral power and odds ratio product (ORP)-based sleep depth in individuals with and without insomnia. We hypothesized that more severe daily dysfunction would be associated with poorer sleep continuity, higher high-frequency EEG activity and lighter sleep depth. The final sample included 859 adults (50.1% female; mean age 44.2 ± 14.1 years) in the Sleep Apnea Global Interdisciplinary Consortium (SAGIC) without obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) or shift work, including 368 with insomnia. EFA supported a single factor underlying the nine daily dysfunction items, which were combined into a total score. In univariate linear regression analyses adjusted for age, sex and site, higher beta-1 power and several ORP measures were nominally associated with more severe daily dysfunction, but none of them survived correction for multiple comparisons. No significant predictor-by-group interactions were observed. Across three levels of sleep physiology-PSG macroarchitecture, spectral power, and continuous sleep depth-no sleep measure was associated with daily dysfunction after correction for multiple comparisons. PSG macroarchitecture and sleep EEG-derived measures may not fully capture daily dysfunction. Future studies could examine whether within-night sleep dynamics are more informative than whole-night averages.

papers.title: Cardiac regulatory and circadian gene expression and antioxidant enzyme activities in cold-exposed Daurian ground squirrels.
papers.abstract: The Daurian ground squirrel (Spermophilus dauricus) is a typical hibernating mammal, exhibiting tolerance to low ambient temperatures. To elucidate the cardiac physiological adaptation mechanisms of animals to cold exposure, the present study investigated the effects of continuous 6-day cold exposure (5 ± 1 °C) on the expression of cardiac functional genes, Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, and antioxidant enzyme activity in summer-active Daurian ground squirrels. Cold exposure significantly reduced the mRNA expression of nNOS, eNOS, Adora1, Adora2A, and Adrb1, while increasing that of Chrm2. It also significantly downregulated the expression of the circadian genes Clock, Cry2, and Per1-3, whereas Cry1 expression was upregulated. The cardiac Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase activity was decreased, while activities of T-AOC, SOD, and CAT in the heart were enhanced, and MDA content increased. These findings suggest that cold exposure may affect cardiac function via circadian genes, NO signaling, and adenosine/adrenergic/cholinergic regulation, while minimizing ion transport energy expenditure and enhancing antioxidant defense.

papers.title: Temporal Associations Between Physiological Sleep and Next-Day Pain Intensity in Individuals With Activity-Limiting Chronic Pain: A Multiple Night At-Home Ear-EEG Sleep-Monitoring Study.
papers.abstract: Chronic pain and sleep disturbances frequently co-occur. However, most prior research relies on self-report or actigraphy, which reflect behavioural aspects of sleep but provide only limited insight into the underlying sleep physiology. In this pre-registered prospective observational study (NCT06368531), we investigated within-person night-to-night variability in physiological sleep metrics and explored temporal associations between sleep metrics and next-day pain. Individuals with bothersome (n = 4) or high-impact (n = 15) chronic pain completed between 11 and 33 nights of at-home sleep monitoring using an ear-EEG device and rated morning pain intensity daily on a 0-10 numerical rating scale. This design enables assessment of real-world physiological sleep patterns alongside natural fluctuations in pain, offering a high-resolution view of sleep-pain dynamics beyond traditional diary or actigraphy-based methods. Substantial between-night variability was observed across multiple sleep metrics, such as sleep efficiency and sleep stage transitions (ICC values < 0.5), indicating that less than half of the total variance was attributable to differences between subjects, underscoring the importance of longitudinal within-person monitoring. Mixed-effects model analyses revealed that lower next-day pain intensity was associated with greater duration (β = -0.01, p = 0.005), higher percentage (β = -0.07, p = 0.001) and increased stability (β = -0.01, p = 0.013) of N3 sleep. In contrast, higher next-day pain was associated with increased N3 fragmentation (β = 0.01, p = 0.014) and a higher proportion of N1 sleep (β = 0.014, p = 0.007). Together, these findings provide objective physiological support for previously reported associations between sleep and pain, highlighting the value of longitudinal ear-EEG monitoring for capturing nightly sleep-pain dynamics. papers.title: Resting-State EEG Spectral Power in Young Adults With Generalized Anxiety Disorder and Self-Reported Habitual Short Sleep: A Case-Control Study.
papers.abstract: Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) and insufficient sleep frequently co-occur during early adulthood, yet resting-state electroencephalographic (EEG) evidence in this population remains limited. The present study aimed to characterize resting-state EEG spectral power in young adults with GAD who also reported habitual short sleep, compared with healthy controls. This exploratory case-control study included 56 university students: 28 participants with GAD and self-reported habitual short sleep and 28 healthy controls. Resting-state EEG spectral power was quantified in the delta, theta, alpha, and beta bands. We retained unadjusted group comparisons for description and fitted age- and sex-adjusted linear models for the primary inferential interpretation. Channel-wise models likewise included group, age, and sex, with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction across the 30 channels within each frequency band. After adjustment for age and sex, group coefficients remained positive for delta (2.51, 95% CI: 0.20 to 4.82), theta (2.52, 95% CI: 0.29 to 4.74), alpha (2.46, 95% CI: -0.12 to 5.03), and beta power (2.14, 95% CI: 0.13 to 4.15), but none met the FDR threshold (adjusted FDR p = 0.0501, 0.0501, 0.0608, and 0.0501, respectively). In unadjusted analyses, delta, theta, and beta differences survived FDR correction (FDR p = 0.0480 for each), whereas alpha did not (FDR p = 0.0553). In adjusted channel-wise analyses, 26 channel-by-band comparisons across 15 channels survived within-band FDR correction; all occurred in delta or theta and were concentrated over posterior and centroparietal electrodes. Whole-scalp estimates were directionally higher in the GAD plus habitual short-sleep group, but no age- and sex-adjusted frequency-band comparison survived FDR correction. Adjusted exploratory channel-wise findings indicated a posterior and centroparietal concentration in delta and theta power. These estimates remain preliminary and do not permit attribution to GAD, habitual short sleep, or their interaction.

papers.title: Poststroke sleep phenotypes and executive dysfunction: toward a sleep-network-executive framework.
papers.abstract: Post-stroke sleep disturbance and executive dysfunction frequently coexist, yet the mechanisms linking disturbed sleep to cognitive recovery remain poorly understood. A major challenge is phenotypic heterogeneity: insomnia, sleep fragmentation, obstructive sleep apnea, hypersomnolence, and circadian disruption differ in their biological drivers and cognitive consequences. To develop a testable network-level account, we conducted a targeted synthesis of clinical stroke studies, stroke neuroimaging research, non-stroke sleep-network evidence, and intervention studies, mapping each evidence stream according to its proximity to the proposed pathway. The synthesis indicates that focal lesions, diaschisis, and structural disconnection after stroke can disrupt the integrity and coordination of the salience, default mode, and frontoparietal networks. Clinical studies support an association between disturbed sleep and poorer post-stroke cognition, while neuroimaging findings demonstrate altered large scale network organization in post-stroke cognitive impairment. Evidence from non-stroke populations further suggests that sleep loss, insomnia, and sleep fragmentation can impair network segregation, default mode regulation, frontoparietal recruitment, and salience-network-mediated switching. We therefore propose that sleep fragmentation, insomnia, and arousal instability may act as functional stressors on an already vulnerable post-stroke network architecture. Inefficient switching may permit context-inappropriate persistence of default mode activity and reduce or delay frontoparietal engagement during executive demand, thereby contributing to impaired conflict monitoring, working memory, processing speed, and cognitive flexibility. No study has directly tested this complete pathway within a single stroke cohort. The framework should therefore be regarded as a falsifiable mechanistic hypothesis rather than an established causal model. Future studies should combine objective sleep phenotyping, dynamic and effective connectivity, task based neuroimaging, domain specific executive measures, and longitudinal or interventional designs within the same stroke cohorts.

papers.title: CK2 and DBT promote temperature compensation of the Drosophila circadian clock via distinct pathways.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythms are defined by three fundamental properties: they are self-sustained, entrained by environmental cues, and temperature compensated. The molecular basis of temperature compensation remains incompletely understood. Here, we found that reducing the activity of two highly conserved circadian kinases, Drosophila doubletime/casein kinase 1 and casein kinase 2 (DBT/CK1 and CK2), compromises temperature compensation in Drosophila melanogaster. Genetic analyses indicate that DBT and CK2 promote temperature compensation through distinct but additive pathways. DBT works through the per Short phosphorylation cluster and the Ser47 phosphodegron of the core clock protein PER, whereas CK2 acts through a phosphocluster in TIM and PER Ser45 residue. Simultaneous disruption of both pathways results in hyperphosphorylated PER accumulation and impaired PER clearance from circadian pacemaker neuron nuclei. Combined with previous studies, our findings support a central role for nuclear PER phosphorylation dynamics in buffering circadian period against environmental temperature fluctuations.

papers.abstract: Circadian rhythms are a fundamental biological process that coordinates physiological functions, behavior, and metabolism with an approximately 24-hour periodicity. At the center of the mammalian circadian timing system is the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus, which generates robust, clock-gated neuronal output that establishes the temporal organization of cellular and physiological processes throughout the body. Our previous work demonstrated that the scaffold protein PEA-15 (phosphoprotein enriched in astrocytes 15) is highly expressed in the SCN and dynamically interacts with ERK, a key effector kinase of the MAPK pathway, to regulate its subcellular localization. Given the important role of ERK/MAPK signaling in circadian timing and photic entrainment, we extended this work using PEA-15 knockout (PEA-15 -/- ) mice to determine how loss of PEA- 15 affects circadian timing, entrainment, and ERK signaling within the SCN. At the cellular level, both clock-gated and light-evoked ERK activation were significantly reduced in PEA- 15 -/- mice compared with wild-type controls. Under constant darkness, PEA-15 -/- mice exhibited a significantly shorter free-running period relative to wild-type animals. Assessment of circadian entrainment using jet-lag resetting and Aschoff type I light-pulse paradigms revealed a blunted phase-delay response to light and an accelerated rate of entrainment to a phase-advancing light stimulus. Thus, loss of PEA-15 alters multiple properties of the SCN clock, including its intrinsic period and its responsiveness to photic input, with effects that depend on the direction of phase resetting. Collectively, these findings identify PEA-15 as an important regulator of SCN circadian function and implicate ERK/MAPK signaling as one mechanism through which PEA-15 modulates clock timing and photic entrainment.

papers.title: Modeling circadian rhythm splitting under chronic light and the asymmetric transition kinetics between lighting conditions
papers.abstract: In various vertebrates, chronic light splits the single daily 24-h circadian activity bout into two 12-h behavioral components per cycle, yet the underlying mechanism remains unresolved. Here, we develop a two-lobe biophysical model of the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) to understand this phenomenon. By representing the master clock as interacting ventral core and dorsal shell populations of Kuramoto-type oscillators across bilateral lobes, we suggest that chronic light changes the excitation/inhibition (E/I) balance orchestrated by GABA, which either inhibits or excites SCN neurons. Under constant darkness, excitation dominates and provides in-phase synchronization of the populations. Under chronic light, inhibition dominates, and the ipsilateral and contralateral couplings among the core and shell populations become negative. Consequently, the shells in the left and right lobes oscillate in antiphase, producing the 12-h behavioral rhythm in downstream tissues. We suggest that this E/I balance is shifted by a light-induced change in the expression of chloride cotransporters in SCN neurons. Another key novelty is the introduction of the biologically motivated dynamics of chloride cotransporter expression, which explains the sign inversion of ipsilateral and contralateral couplings under time-varying lighting conditions. The model also reproduces the effects of unilateral SCN lesions: if one lobe is abolished, the remaining intact lobe autonomously stabilizes into a single-bout circadian output with a period comparable to that of the intact system. Finally, we compare our results with experimental data and demonstrate a close agreement.

papers.title: Tryptophan metabolism circadian regulation: clinical and pharmacological implications.
papers.abstract: Circadian clocks are endogenous systems that synchronize physiology and behavior to the light-dark cycle, regulating sleep-wake timing, hormonal rhythms, metabolism and immunity. Among metabolic pathways tightly linked to circadian rhythm, tryptophan (Trp) metabolism occupies a central position because its catabolism through the kynurenine (Kyn) pathway, the serotonin (5-HT)-melatonin pathway and the microbiota-derived indole-AhR pathway, produce molecules endowed with significant neuro-modulatory and immunoregulatory activities and directly involved in circadian regulation. Emerging evidence supports a bidirectional relationship between the clock system and Trp metabolism. The molecular clock regulates expression and activity of key Trp enzymes, creating time-of-day variation in Trp flux, Kyn-Trp ratio, serotonin/melatonin synthesis and AhR ligands availability. Conversely, Trp-derived metabolites in turn modulate clock function and downstream physiology, such as diurnal variations in metabolism and immune response. Here we discuss recent studies highlighting how this interplay has important pathophysiological implications and disruption of Trp metabolism oscillatory pattern influences our susceptibility to developing diseases, such as infectious, metabolic and neuropsychiatric diseases. Moreover, we highlight the importance of considering daily fluctuation when using these molecules as biomarkers and interpreting them in a clinical setting. Among circadian-based interventions, such as chronotherapy, light therapy or time-restricted feeding, we propose pharmacological targeting of Trp pathways or pharmacological use of Trp derivatives as a novel approach of circadian medicine, able to improve clinical outcomes across various fields.

papers.title: Feedback Valence, Prediction Error, and the Limits of Computational Attribution in Symptom-Related EEG
papers.abstract: Feedback-locked electroencephalography (EEG) responses are often interpreted using model-derived prediction errors (PEs), although signed PE can be strongly coupled to feedback valence in binary-outcome tasks. We revisited a published anxiety-related EEG association using two open probabilistic-learning datasets to examine measurement reliability, predictor separability, and participant-level recovery. In the primary dataset, greater trait anxiety was associated with a larger negative-minus-positive FCz theta response among 46 participants with elevated depressive symptoms after adjustment for depression severity. The association also differed between the sampled depression-symptom groups. The feedback contrast showed useful within-session reliability, but matched delta and P3-minus-N2 analyses did not establish theta specificity. Within participants, feedback valence and signed PE were highly correlated (r = -0.964). Exact-design simulations showed that population-level model discrimination could succeed despite poor recovery of individual neural slopes. Participant-specific learning-model refits recovered overall signed PE more consistently than the within-valence variation needed to distinguish it from feedback valence. An independent dataset reproduced the FCz feedback contrast in untreated and placebo cohorts but lacked trait-anxiety scores. Adding signed PE to valence yielded a small held-out predictive improvement under one reinforcement-learning specification, with limited support across sessions and no comparable support under the dual-rate model or in placebo. Together, these findings support a symptom-related feedback EEG association while constraining its theta-specific and participant-level computational interpretation.

papers.title: Respiratory control instability during sleep is associated with incident atrial fibrillation.
papers.abstract: There is an association between central sleep apnea (CSA) and atrial fibrillation (AF). However, standard scoring and threshold criteria for CSA are relatively rigid and does not capture the entirety of expressed high loop gain (HLG) of the respiratory control system during sleep. We aimed to investigate the association between HLG sleep apnea, as measured by a respiratory self-similarity (SS) detection algorithm, and the risk of incident AF. Polysomnograms from the Sleep Heart Health Study (SHHS) and the Osteoporotic Fractures in Men Study (MrOS) were analyzed to quantify expressed HLG using an automated algorithm that calculates SS% and a Central Respiratory Event Index (CREI). Multivariable Logistic regression models were used to assess the relationship between HLG metrics and incident AF. A total of 3706 participants (2897 from SHHS and 809 from MrOS) were included. In MrOS, high SS% (≥13.5%) and high CREI (≥30 events/hour) remained significantly associated with incident AF after mutual adjustment with CSA (SS%: OR 1.697, 95% CI 1.027-2.805, p: 0.039; CREI: OR 1.661, 95% CI 1.022-2.699, p: 0.041). In SHHS participants <65 years, SS% >10.5% was associated with AF after full adjustment (OR 3.613, 95% CI 1.347-9.693, p: 0.011) and remained significant after adjustment for CSA (OR 7.661, 95% CI 1.875-31.309, p: 0.005). Expressed high loop gain sleep apnea is independently associated with incident atrial fibrillation in community-based cohorts.

papers.title: Multi-Modal Wearable and Biological Data Integration Reveals Physiological Signatures of Weight Variation in Overweight and Obese Adults: An AI4Food Machine Learning Study
papers.abstract: This study is part of the AI4Food project, which aims to identify the physiological and behavioral factors influencing weight variation in overweight and obese individuals through integrative analysis of multi-source data. A 30-day crossover intervention was conducted on 93 participants at IMDEA Nutrition Institute, combining a traditional phase (questionnaires, food diaries) and a digital phase (Fitbit Sense Smartwatch, FreeStyle Libre 2 glucose sensor). The collected data encompassed sleep, glucose, skin temperature, nutrition, and gut microbiome information. After rigorous preprocessing and alignment by intervention days, unsupervised clustering, association analysis, and machine learning models were applied to uncover physiological patterns linked to weight dynamics. Results showed greater weight reduction during the digital phase in Group 2, while between-group differences were not significant. Significant associations were observed between nocturnal respiratory rate, skin temperature, and weight variation. Under participant-level five-fold cross-validation, Random Forest models achieved mean accuracies of 64.3% for thermoregulation and 61.7% for glucose phenotype prediction, with RMSSD, restlessness, and nocturnal respiratory rate among the most influential predictors. In contrast, microbiome composition remained almost stable over the short intervention period. These findings support the potential of AI-driven integration of wearable and nutritional data to stratify metabolic phenotypes and advance personalized nutrition strategies in obesity management.

papers.title: Enlightening pregnancy as a potential pathway to protect maternal circadian functioning and postpartum mood.
papers.abstract: The perinatal period is characterized by profound psychological, physiological, and behavioral changes that may increase sleep, circadian, and affective disturbances. While sleep disruption across pregnancy and postpartum has been widely documented, far less is known about how this transition shapes circadian health and whether circadian characteristics during pregnancy predict postpartum circadian and affective outcomes. In this study, we characterize circadian preference, circadian phase, circadian function, and light exposure across the transition from late pregnancy to early postpartum, and examine their predictive value for postpartum circadian function and depressive and anxiety symptomatology. Women were followed from the third trimester of pregnancy to 1 month postpartum. At both time points, participants wore a wrist actigraph to derive circadian parameters including the circadian function index (CFI) and circadian phase (L5c), and to quantify mean light exposure. Circadian preference and affective states were also assessed by questionnaires (MEQ, EPDS, STAI-T). Within-subject changes from pregnancy to postpartum were examined, and regression models were used to test whether prenatal circadian and affective measures predicted postpartum circadian function and depressive symptomatology. The transition to postpartum was marked by a significant reduction in CFI and mean light exposure, whereas circadian preference and L5c remained largely stable. During pregnancy, higher CFI was associated with morningness and greater light exposure; however, these associations were no longer evident postpartum. Postpartum CFI was predicted by prenatal CFI and circadian preference, with lower values observed among women with more evening-oriented profiles. In parallel, prenatal affective symptoms showed continuity into the postpartum period, and both prenatal CFI and circadian preference contributed to the prediction of postpartum depressive symptoms. Together, these findings indicate that early postpartum is characterized by a decay in circadian function rather than a shift in circadian phase, identify eveningness as a vulnerability factor during the transition to motherhood, support the use of CFI as an integrative marker of maternal circadian health, and highlight pregnancy as a potential window for circadian-informed interventions aimed at improving postpartum circadian and mood outcomes.

papers.title: Rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder as a model of early neurodegeneration: challenges for research and clinical diagnosis.
papers.abstract: Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder (RBD) has evolved from a descriptive parasomnia to a clinically informative model for studying early neurodegenerative processes, particularly within the spectrum of α-synucleinopathies. Defined by the loss of REM sleep atonia and the emergence of dream enactment behaviors, RBD reflects dysfunction of brainstem circuits that normally suppress motor output during dreaming. Longitudinal evidence indicates that many individuals with isolated RBD eventually develop neurodegenerative disease, most commonly Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, or, less frequently, multiple system atrophy, positioning RBD among the most specific clinical markers of prodromal synucleinopathy currently recognized. Mechanistic studies suggest that RBD arises from instability within distributed REM sleep regulatory networks involving dopaminergic, noradrenergic, serotonergic, and cholinergic systems. This network dysfunction may precede classic motor and cognitive symptoms and can be accompanied by early abnormalities in neurophysiology, imaging, cognition, olfaction, autonomic function, and molecular biomarkers. These findings support a model in which RBD may represent one of the earliest clinically accessible manifestations of a multisystem neurodegenerative process, although anatomical origin, propagation patterns, and phenoconversion trajectories vary across patients. Despite these advances, clinical management remains largely symptomatic, and key challenges persist in diagnosis, risk stratification, prognostic counselling, and therapeutic development. A broader clinical framework is therefore needed, in which RBD is not viewed solely as an isolated sleep disorder but also as a potential marker of early neurodegeneration in appropriately characterized patients. Integrating polysomnography with multimodal biomarkers and network-based models of disease may refine risk stratification and support the development of targeted interventions at earlier stages of neurodegenerative disease.

papers.title: Pathophysiology of REM sleep behaviour disorder.
papers.abstract: REM sleep behaviour disorder (RBD) is a parasomnia characterized by loss of muscle atonia and dream enactment behaviour during REM sleep. Additionally, RBD is not a terminal illness, and data generalisability is limited by the high co-occurrence of α-synucleinopathies. In this review, we discuss the mechanisms responsible for altered REM sleep regulation in RBD, incorporating evidence from human post-mortem histological analyses, structural and functional neuroimaging data on patients with RBD, and pharmacological studies. We explore the risks, biomarkers, and mechanisms of phenoconversion from RBD to α-synucleinopathies, drawing on data from large longitudinal patient cohorts, and we consider disease remission. The primary outcome was the cumulative hydromorphone consumption during the first 24 h after surgery. papers.title: Participant-Disjoint EEG Decoding of Instructed Respiratory Conditions Using a Deep Spatio-Respiratory Transformer.
papers.abstract: Fine-grained classification of instructed respiratory conditions from non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) remains challenging because of low signal-to-noise ratio and substantial inter-participant variability. This study proposes a Deep Spatio-Respiratory Transformer (DSRT) for EEG-based classification of instructed respiratory conditions. DSRT integrates differential entropy (DE) and normalized power-ratio (NPR) features, squeeze-and-excitation-based feature recalibration, a four-layer feature-token Transformer encoder, and auxiliary nasal/oral pathway supervision. The final task comprised eight respiratory-condition classes. The framework was evaluated using 64-channel EEG from 13 unique participants contributing 21 recording sessions. A fixed-count window-selection strategy was used to equalize the number of retained EEG windows across classes, and model evaluation was performed using participant-disjoint outer folds. Primary architecture comparisons and feature-representation analyses were conducted using participant-level performance summaries. At the participant level, DSRT achieved an Accuracy of 0.7429 ± 0.0492. Compared with EEG Conformer, the strongest matched-input comparison architecture, DSRT improved Accuracy and Macro-F1 by 3.78 and 3.79 percentage points, respectively. Architectural ablation showed the largest performance reduction after removal of the Transformer encoder, while participant-level feature-sensitivity analysis showed that the combined DE-NPR representation outperformed either feature family alone. DSRT contained 1.297 million parameters and achieved a median window-to-prediction latency of 3.825 ms. Duration-matched analysis further identified spatially heterogeneous EEG differences associated with instructed nasal and oral breathing. DSRT provides a participant-disjoint framework for fine-grained classification of EEG patterns associated with instructed respiratory conditions while retaining millisecond-scale inference. The findings support the utility of hybrid spectral representations and feature-token dependency modeling.

papers.title: Sleep components, depressive subdomains and quality of life in Parkinson's disease: A cross-sectional exploratory analysis.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances and depressive symptoms are prevalent non-motor burdens in Parkinson's disease (PD) and are closely associated with poorer health-related quality of life (QoL). Non-motor symptoms of PD exhibit substantial heterogeneity. It remains unclear whether distinct sleep disturbances show differential correlations with physical and mental QoL, and whether specific depressive subdimensions are implicated in these relationships. This exploratory study analyzed direct and indirect associations among sleep components, depressive subdimensions, and physical-mental QoL in hospitalized patients with PD. This retrospective study analyzed data from 55 hospitalized patients with idiopathic PD who completed the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), the 24-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAMD), the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), and the 36-Item Short Form Health Survey (SF-36). Spearman correlation and multivariable regression analyses were performed to assess bivariate associations and independent correlates of QoL. Exploratory PROCESS analyses were further implemented as hypothesis-generating secondary analyses to examine symptom-level indirect associations; all findings were interpreted as cross-sectional and non-causal. Spearman correlation analyses showed that the PSQI total score was significantly correlated with both PCS and MCS (both p < 0.01). These preliminary findings underline the heterogeneity of PD non-motor symptoms and provide a hypothesis-generating framework for future longitudinal validation and targeted intervention studies.

The attacks were occipital-suboccipital, pulsating and pressure-like, rated 7/10 in intensity, and accompanied by scalp allodynia, bilateral conjunctival hyperemia and lacrimation, mild nasal congestion, and restlessness. Neurologic examination and investigations for secondary causes were unremarkable. Serial brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated a benign-appearing pineal cyst measuring initially 21 × 11 × 10 mm, without hydrocephalus, obstruction of cerebrospinal fluid pathways, or aggressive radiologic features. Treatment with oral melatonin at 4 mg nightly reduced the headache symptoms by approximately 50% within four weeks. Increasing the dose to 8 mg nightly was followed by complete resolution within six weeks. papers.abstract: This study aimed to explore differences in demographic, clinical, and psychological characteristics among middle-aged and elderly Chinese patients with moderate-to-severe sleep-disordered breathing (SDB) across educational levels, and to identify factors associated with the oxygen desaturation index (ODI) as well as potential statistical indirect effects. We further examined whether educational level moderates the relationship between psychological symptoms and ODI. A total of 306 patients with moderate-to-severe SDB were recruited with strict exclusion criteria. All participants underwent overnight monitoring with a wrist pulse oximeter to calculate ODI (oxygen desaturation events ≥3% lasting ≥3 s per hour). Demographic information, medical history, and questionnaire scores (sleepiness, insomnia, anxiety, depression, fatigue, quality of life) were collected. Patients were divided into lower (primary school or unschooled) and higher (junior high school or above) educational level groups. A predefined multivariable linear regression model and statistical mediation analysis were used. Age- and sex-adjusted group comparisons were performed. Among 306 patients, 178 were in the lower educational level group and 128 in the higher educational level group. After age and sex adjustment, the higher educational level group had higher ODI, BMI, monthly income, alcohol use, daytime sleepiness, insomnia, anxiety, and depression scores, but less fatigue. Educational level was not independently associated with ODI after multivariable adjustment. In the overall sample, BMI (standardized beta = 0.252, P < 0.001) and average monthly income (standardized beta = 0.24, P = 0.001) were independent correlates of ODI. BMI statistically accounted for 27.3% of the association between average monthly income and ODI. Subgroup analyses using the predefined regression model showed that GAD-7 anxiety score was positively associated with ODI in the lower educational level group (standardized beta = 0.372, P < 0.05), while BMI (standardized beta = 0.324, P = 0.002) and average monthly income (standardized beta = 0.219, P = 0.048) were positively associated with ODI in the higher educational level group. The higher education subgroup findings were consistent with the overall sample results. Educational level is not directly associated with ODI but stratifies distinct clinical and psychological profiles and heterogeneous ODI-associated factors in patients with SDB. In the lower education group, anxiety (GAD-7) emerges as an independent correlate of ODI, while in the higher education group, BMI and income predominate, findings consistent with the overall sample. BMI and income are independent correlates with ODI, with BMI statistically accounting for a portion of the income-ODI association. These cross-sectional findings highlight the need for education-stratified approaches to SDB assessment, with particular attention to anxiety symptoms in lower-educated populations.

papers.title: Integrating uncertainty and practice variability for epilepsy prognostication after intracranial EEG: A meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: Intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) practices and diagnostic testing vary among institutions, limiting standardization and optimization of surgical outcomes. This study estimates resection rates and surgical outcome effect sizes after iEEG and develops individual patient-level data (IPD) models using the missing-indicator method to approximate real-world clinical uncertainties and practice variability in iEEG and surgical decision-making. Databases were queried for studies reporting ≥12-month outcomes after epilepsy surgery in patients with drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE) who underwent iEEG. Random-effects meta-analysis estimated pooled outcome proportions. IPD analysis was performed using multivariable generalized linear regression and logistic regression models with cross-validation and calibration assessment. Missing values for key predictors were retained as a "not specified" category to evaluate the impact of incorporating uncertainty in common clinical data on outcome prediction. Primary outcomes were seizure freedom (Engel class IA or International League Against Epilepsy [ILAE] 1) and favorable seizure outcomes (Engel I or ILAE 1-2). Of 4975 studies identified, 115 met the inclusion criteria. The pooled frequency of patients undergoing resection after iEEG was 67% (95% confidence interval [CI] 60%-74%), 52% achieved seizure freedom (95% CI 48%-56%), and 58% achieved a favorable outcome (95% CI 54%-62%). IPD analysis included 1305 patients from 29 studies and identified a lesional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI; odds ratio [OR] 1.94, CI 1.48-2.55, p < .0001) and a cortical malformation (OR 1.47, CI 1.08-2.00, p = .01) as independent predictors of a favorable outcome, whereas iEEG implantation strategy (bilateral implantation OR .61, 95% CI .42-.89, p = .01) was an independent predictor of a less favorable outcome. About two-thirds of patients undergoing iEEG proceeded to resection, and about half achieved seizure freedom. Multivariable models incorporating clinical uncertainty and practice variability were well calibrated. However, modest discrimination suggests that routinely available clinical variables alone have limited ability to predict individual surgical outcomes. More standardized and granular clinical and practice-related data may improve individualized prognostication after iEEG.

papers.title: Personalized Postoperative Pain Management and Therapies Based on Pharmacogenomics.
papers.abstract: Postoperative pain management must account for differences in drug metabolism, pain phenotype, prior opioid exposure, psychosocial vulnerability, and cognitive function. This narrative review proposes a staged precision-medicine framework separating clinically actionable pharmacogenomics from heterogeneous risk modifiers and investigational adjuncts. The strongest actionable guidance concerns CYP2D6-guided codeine and tramadol prescribing. Other genetic markers require interpretation alongside procedure-specific pain, comorbidities, medication exposure, and patient preferences rather than use as deterministic prescribing rules. Dopamine-related pathways provide a mechanistic link between pain, reward, motivation, and attention. Parkinson disease illustrates dopamine-pain interactions but is not a direct model of postoperative pain. Reward Deficiency Syndrome, the Genetic Addiction Risk Severity/Score, and the Reward Deficiency Syndrome Questionnaire-29 are considered exploratory constructs rather than validated tools for postoperative prescribing. The Continuous Visual Attention Test may offer objective neurocognitive monitoring through reaction time, response variability, and error measures. These measures are not pain-specific and require interpretation in the context of anesthesia, opioids, sedatives, sleep disruption, mood, delirium, baseline cognition, and pain intensity. Prospective studies should determine whether integrating clinical assessment, established pharmacogenomic guidance, and investigational behavioral and neurocognitive measures improves pain outcomes, opioid requirements, adherence, functional recovery, and safety. The framework defines research priorities and implementation endpoints while preserving multimodal analgesia, opioid stewardship, and clinical judgment as the foundation of care.

papers.title: Temporal coupling shapes the effects of prolonged muscle-tendon vibration on sensorimotor EEG activity during motor imagery.
papers.abstract: Motor imagery (MI) recruits sensorimotor networks overlapping those engaged during physical execution and represents a promising rehabilitation tool. While concurrent afferent stimulation enhances MI-related cortical engagement, the effects of prolonged proprioceptive conditioning prior to MI remain unexplored. This study investigated whether prolonged muscle-tendon vibration (MTV) could modulate cortical activity during subsequent MI, indexed by electroencephalographic alpha- and beta-band event-related desynchronization (ERD). Twenty healthy adults performed imagined maximal isometric knee extensions before and after 20-minute suprapatellar MTV (100 Hz) or SHAM vibration (30 Hz with foam interface) in counterbalanced sessions. Cortical engagement was assessed via EEG burst detection over central electrodes (C3, Cz, C4). Maximal force capacity, submaximal force estimation performance, and cortical responses during combined MI and MTV were also evaluated. MTV induced stronger vibratory responses than SHAM, consistent with enhanced proprioceptive afferent activation. Following MTV, voluntary force outcomes showed near-threshold changes consistent with the expected direction, namely reduced maximal force capacity and altered submaximal force calibration, suggesting modified proprioceptive feedback. MI performed after MTV conditioning exhibited reduced alpha- and beta-band ERD compared to SHAM, with greater vibratory-induced responses being associated with a less pronounced post-vibration beta ERD. Conversely, when MI was performed concurrently with MTV following conditioning, alpha-band ERD increased selectively in the MTV session, with no modulation in the beta band. These findings suggest that prolonged proprioceptive conditioning modulates MI-related cortical engagement differently depending on the sensorimotor context in which imagery is performed. Such state-dependent effects may support distinct intervention strategies aimed either at recalibrating maladaptive sensorimotor patterns or at enhancing cortical recruitment in rehabilitation contexts.

papers.title: Rapidly progressive cognitive decline and drug-induced encephalopathy secondary to teprotumumab for thyroid eye disease: a case report and narrative literature review.
papers.abstract: Teprotumumab, a fully human monoclonal antibody targeting insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor (IGF-1R), is an approved targeted therapy for thyroid eye disease (TED). Teprotumumab-associated encephalopathy is an extremely rare but potentially severe central nervous system adverse event, with only three cases reported globally to date. We report the first Han-Chinese patient with Graves' disease and associated TED complicated by teprotumumab-associated encephalopathy, together with a narrative review of all published cases, to raise clinicians' awareness and improve early recognition and management of this rare complication. A 56-year-old Chinese man with Graves' disease and TED developed acute progressive apathy and encephalopathy characterised by multidomain cognitive and behavioral dysfunction 20 days after the third teprotumumab infusion, with an admission MMSE score of 15. Contrast-enhanced brain MRI, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination, and autoimmune encephalitis antibody screening were unremarkable. Prolonged video-electroencephalography(VEEG) demonstrated intermittent diffuse bilateral slow-wave activity, and widespread interictal epileptiform discharges without electrographic or clinical seizures. Systematic workup excluded infectious, autoimmune, metabolic, and psychiatric encephalopathy. Treatment-emergent hyperglycemia was confirmed as a secondary aggravating factor rather than the primary cause. The patient achieved prominent neurological recovery after individualized treapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) and symptomatic management, with a Naranjo score of 6 indicating probable drug-related encephalopathy. Synthesis of all three previously published teprotumumab-associated encephalopathy cases demonstrates that neurological toxicity can develop as early as the third infusion cycle. These cases present consistent neuroimaging features with variable CSF profiles, and thyroid autoantibody elevation predominantly reflects pre-existing Graves' disease-related autoimmune background instead of directly mediating neurotoxicity. TPE generally facilitates neurological recovery but may be complicated by procedural hypersensitivity and fluctuating therapeutic responses. Notably, interictal epileptiform discharges on VEEG represent a newly identified neurophysiological manifestation of this rare adverse event. A three-hit interacting pathogenic hypothesis is proposed: impaired IGF-1R-dependent neurotrophic signalling serves as the core injury mechanism, while underlying thyroid autoimmunity and treatment-related metabolic disturbance act as susceptibility-modifying factors. This case expands the ethnic and clinical spectrum of teprotumumab-related encephalopathy. Diffuse interictal epileptiform discharges without ictal changes reflect reactive cortical hyperexcitability secondary to acute encephalopathy. Metabolic disturbance merely exacerbated neurological impairment. Limitations include single-case constraints, simultaneous multi-intervention therapy, and lack of direct intracranial mechanistic evidence. Teprotumumab-associated encephalopathy is a rare but serious adverse event. Close neurological surveillance and are essential during medication. Accumulated cases are needed to establish unified diagnostic and therapeutic criteria.

papers.title: Decomposing health inequality by dimensions and determinants in China using EQ-5D-5L: an integrated framework.
papers.abstract: The EQ-5D-5L is a widely used measure of health status that has been increasingly applied to study health inequalities. Despite growing recognition of health as a multidimensional construct, few decomposition studies have simultaneously considered both health dimension and their determinants as sources of inequality. This study fills this gap by providing the first integrated decomposition of socioeconomic-related health inequality in China using the EQ-5D-5L instrument. Using cross-sectional data from a nationally distributed sample of 29,882 Chinese adults, we applied the Erreygers-corrected concentration index (ECI) to measure socioeconomic inequality in EQ-5D-5L utility scores, with household income as the ranking variable. An integrated decomposition framework was developed to jointly quantify the contributions of the five EQ-5D-5L dimensions and their associated determinants to overall health inequality. This framework not only identifies the leading dimensions and determinants but also quantifies how determinants contribute to overall inequality through specific dimensions. The estimated ECI for overall EQ-5D-5L utility scores was 0.0275 (95% confidence interval: 0.0227, 0.0326), indicating modest but statistically significant pro-rich inequality in overall health. Pain/discomfort (PD) and mobility (MO) dimensions jointly accounted for more than 60% of overall inequality. Household income and chronic disease history were primary determinants, which contributed through all five dimensions. Sex-age composition contributed positively to overall inequality but showed an offsetting association with inequality in the anxiety/depression (AD) dimension. Negative life events contributed mainly through the AD and PD dimensions, whereas education was associated with reduced overall inequality via the AD dimension. High malnutrition risk contributed to overall inequality primarily through the MO, usual activities (UA), and SC dimensions, while poor sleep quality contributed predominantly through the AD and PD dimensions. These results were robust to using the Wagstaff-corrected concentration index and an alternative decomposition specification. The contributions of leading determinants to socioeconomic-related health inequality exhibited substantial heterogeneity across health dimensions. Our findings highlight the importance of moving beyond aggregate measures and suggest that interventions informed by the specific determinants and dimensions contributing most to overall inequality may help support more equitable health outcomes in China and other low- and middle-income countries.

papers.title: Tetramelic Monodactyly With Neonatal Encephalopathy: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Congenital limb defects are etiologically heterogeneous congenital malformations, with genetic causes being one of the major contributors. We report a neonate with limb anomalies and severe encephalopathy in whom rapid trio whole-genome sequencing identified a pathogenic duplication at 10q24.31q24.32. A near-term male neonate presented with bilateral radial and tibial ray aplasia, with preserved ulnar and fibular elements, resulting in tetramelic monodactyly of the fifth digits. Family history revealed an apparent autosomal dominant pattern, with the patient's father and older sister similarly affected. In the first days of life, the patient developed unexplained apnea, respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation, and severe diffuse encephalopathy on continuous EEG monitoring. Brain MRI, head ultrasound, and metabolic workup were unremarkable. Echocardiography showed normal cardiac anatomy. Trio rapid whole-genome sequencing demonstrated a 10q24 duplication, a locus previously associated with split-hand/foot malformation. This genetic variant in this family leads to tetramelic monodactyly of the fifth digits across at least two generations.

papers.title: Sleep duration: a neglected factor in stroke prevention among individuals with dysglycemia.
papers.abstract: Stroke imposes a staggering and escalating disease burden in China. Individuals with dysglycemia face a markedly elevated risk of incident cerebrovascular events. This study aimed to characterize global and Chinese trends in stroke burden and examine the association between sleep duration and stroke among individuals with dysglycemia, with a particular focus on the potential utility of sleep duration as an behavioral marker for cerebrovascular risk assessment. This study utilized the Global Burden of Disease 2023 database to assess the trends of stroke burden globally and in China(1990-2023). In addition, the study was conducted using data from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS), encompassing participants aged ≥ 45 with baseline dysglycemia and no prior stroke. Sleep duration was obtained from the 2020 survey, while incident stroke status was ascertained across the 2013, 2015, 2018, and 2020 follow-up waves. Stepwise logistic regression models were employed to evaluate the independent association between baseline sleep duration and new-onset stroke. Restricted cubic splines (RCS) with four knots were applied to explore non-linear dose-response relationships. Additionally, subgroup analyses were conducted to identify effect modifications, and receiver operating characteristic curves evaluated the discriminatory performance of the prediction model including sleep factors. Despite declining global age-standardized rate, the absolute stroke burden in China significantly increased from 1990 to 2023, particularly among males and older adults. In the CHARLS cohort, 7,274 patients with dysglycemia were included in 2011. After a ten-year follow-up, 694 participants (9.54%) developed new strokes. Notably, the sleep duration was significantly longer (9.95 ± 1.74 h hours, P < 0.0001) in the new stroke group. The model after including covariates showed that for every additional hour of sleep, the risk of stroke increased by 22% (OR = 1.22, 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.13-1.32). Crucially, RCS analysis uncovered a non-linear inflection point at 7.5-8 h, demonstrating that cerebrovascular risk accelerated rapidly beyond this threshold. The fully adjusted model showed the highest discriminatory performance among the evaluated models, although the overall discrimination remained modest (AUC = 0.666). China's absolute stroke burden continued to surge. Sleep duration may serve as an easily obtainable behavioral marker that complements conventional factors in stroke risk assessment among individuals with dysglycemia.A non-linear association was observed, with stroke risk increasing more rapidly beyond approximately 7.5-8 h of sleep. These findings suggest that sleep duration may provide complementary information for identifying metabolically vulnerable individuals at elevated cerebrovascular risk, although further prospective validation is required. By synergizing human epidemiological expertise with data-driven modeling, this study may provide a feasible approach to complement stroke risk stratification in metabolically vulnerable populations.

Pooled calibration error falls as accuracy falls, so the headline reliability metric improves as the model degrades. Under transfer, class-balanced calibration error rises by 0.107 to 0.254 in all fifteen model-corpus cells, where coverage falls below its 0.90 target, to 0.533 at worst, with empty prediction sets in four. papers.title: Organised streaming of cerebrospinal fluid in the human third ventricle
papers.abstract: Quasi-periodic pressure pulses associated with cardiac and respiratory activity generate reciprocating cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) motion in the human ventricles. Regular waves dominated by the cardiac cycle are overlaid with cycles of low-frequency respiratory waves, the latter to become stronger in forced breathing or even dominated by large successive flushes in NREM sleep. The present study investigates how such waves contribute to residual streaming within the human ventricles. Transient CFD simulations were performed in the third ventricle at varying parameters of frequency, stroke volume and wave-form asymmetry. Increasing the aqueduct peak Reynolds-number, either by small stroke volume and high frequency or large stroke volume at low frequency, transfers the flow from a reversible flow pattern to the formation of clear preferential pathways, alternating between the in- and outflow cycle. The resulting permanent streaming flux across the aqueduct relative to the mean oscillatory flow-rate, i.e. the dimensionless streaming ratio SR follows a rational saturation relation, SR [~] ReAq,peak/(C + ReAq,peak), demonstrating that increasing the peak aqueduct Reynolds number yields diminishing returns and bounds the relative contribution of residual inter-ventricular streaming. These findings demonstrate differences in hydrodynamic organisation in the third ventricle and highlight the importance of this organisation for intraventricular fluid exchange.
